public_rationale: The ordinary reading is that negation was a substantial recurring weakness, not an absolute inability. Contemporary evaluations found substantial losses when negation mattered to the answer. Context-sensitive successes qualify the breadth of the claim without eliminating that weakness. See the [performance study](https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-short.81.pdf) and the [pragmatic-context study](https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-long.315/).
limitations: Support is strongest for the tested transformer models and tasks.
The evidence does not justify saying that all neural networks ignored no and not.
Conference evidence is recorded as available by the final conference day; the supporting study also had a March preprint.

our_interpretation: The language-acquisition context makes neural language models the relevant class of networks.
A major sore spot means substantial, recurring difficulty interpreting negation. It does not mean every model fails whenever negation appears.
Because the statement describes an ongoing research state without a reporting interval, the target period is the current research year through publication: January 1 to July 20, 2022.
Comparisons must concern understanding negation, rather than merely detecting the presence of a negative word.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporary evaluations show substantial, recurring errors when negation matters to the answer, with materially worse results than relevant affirmative or nonessential-negation comparisons.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative contemporary models handle meaning-changing negation reliably across varied tasks, with little meaningful disadvantage against comparable cases without negation.

evidence.locator: Table 4 caption; section 3, research question Q3
evidence.explanation: The study reports substantial RoBERTa performance losses on subsets where negation matters: QNLI macro F1 is 0.67 for important negations versus 0.92 for unimportant negations. These are dataset-subset comparisons, not matched sentence pairs; the findings were already reported in the March preprint.

The authors report a substantially more optimistic assessment from pragmatic tests of transformer models. This is material counterevidence to a universal inability claim, but does not establish reliable performance across the tasks implicated by e1.
